sources.title: History
sources.annotation: Read the complete substantive history page, including its contemporary self-description and church affiliations. It presents the organization’s own account of identity and continuity alongside quotations from older writers. Useful as community public history, with historical priority, land-title, genealogy and broad Caddoan-language claims requiring separate verification. The general About directory is not an additional resource.

sources.title: Programs & Services
sources.annotation: Read the complete page. Describes language reconstruction, seminars, field trips and volunteer emergency services. Dictionary and children’s-book projects are described as underway. The page’s categorical Caddoan classification is not adopted as linguistic consensus. Listed equipment is reported capacity, not an independent readiness audit; page sections and links do not count as separate works.

sources.title: Bylaws of Caddo Adais Indians, Inc.
sources.publisher: Caddo Adais Indians, Inc. / Adai Caddo Indian Nation
sources.annotation: Read PDF pages 1–10 of 12, including Articles I–II, IV, VI and VIII–IX. The document states a March 2, 2024 revision and effective date. It identifies the corporation and its Adai Caddo public name, council responsibilities, elections, elders and appointed roles. These are published institutional rules, not a federal acknowledgment decision or proof of unchanged historical government.

sources.title: Introducing the Adai Indian Nation
sources.publisher: Morgan, Angel & Associates, LLC; digital copy at the Newberry Library
sources.annotation: Read pages 1–7 and 15–19 of the 19-page briefing. Michael L. Lawson prepared it in cooperation with Chief Rufus Davis and anthropologist Maria D. Wade. Its community-collaborative account discusses dispersed relatives, work migration, church and homecoming. Undated; PDF creation metadata does not establish publication date. Recognition arguments are advocacy; inconsistent grant/cession dates are not used. This is not an agency determination.
sources.author: Michael L. Lawson, in cooperation with Rufus Davis and Maria D. Wade

sources.title: Adai Caddo Indian Nation holds 2nd Annual Field Trip visiting sites across Natchitoches and CENLA
sources.annotation: Read the complete March 31, 2026 report and visually checked all three pages of the tribal-hosted archived screenshots. Reports a March field trip and quotes organizer Robert Brevelle and historian Dee Niette Thompson. Evidence for a reported educational activity and participants’ aims; historical site identifications, genealogy and land-ownership assertions are not independently established here. Original article and archived PDF are one work.

sources.title: Native America Calling — May 28, 2025 Adai interview transcript
sources.publisher: Native America Calling / Koahnic Broadcast Corporation; transcript posted by Adai Caddo Indian Nation
sources.annotation: Read all six pages of the tribal-posted transcript of Shawn Spruce’s interview with council member Robert Brevelle; also checked the official episode page. Brevelle discusses acknowledgment, elder health, youth education and cultural preservation. These are attributed priorities and advocacy, not proof of petition status, eligibility or funding received. Recording not independently audited against this transcript; other episode interviews are not represented as reviewed.
sources.author: Shawn Spruce (host); Robert Brevelle (interviewee)

supportingSources.title: Government — Great Seal interpretation
supportingSources.annotation: Read the complete government page and public explanation of the seal, attributed to Paige Holsapple and Robert Brevelle. The community interprets particular motifs through its own history and faith. Short supporting interpretation, kept outside the six-source count. It does not establish universal Caddo symbolism, historical title or the historical accuracy of every association.

supportingSources.title: Cultural Center
supportingSources.annotation: Read the complete short page: public museum/exhibit and meeting-facility description, photographs and published street address. Supporting visitor and geographic information only. It supplies a present facility location, not a historical homeland boundary. The community publishes LA-485, while the state directory prints LA-486; no coordinates were inferred from the conflicting roads.

supportingSources.title: Federally and State-Recognized Tribes
supportingSources.publisher: Louisiana Office of the Governor / Indian Affairs
supportingSources.annotation: Read the federal and state headings and Adai entry on the live official directory on October 20, 2026. It places “Adai Caddo Indians of Louisiana” under State Recognized Tribes. Supports that precisely attributed listing, without establishing its legal origin date, federal status or equivalence to another Caddo government. Name/contact listing kept outside the substantive-source count.

supportingSources.title: Indian Entities Recognized by and Eligible To Receive Services From the United States Bureau of Indian Affairs
supportingSources.publisher: Bureau of Indian Affairs; Federal Register / Government Publishing Office
supportingSources.annotation: Read the notice introduction and relevant alphabetical entries in the official five-page PDF, 91 FR 4102–4106, and searched its complete extracted text. Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is listed; Adai/Adais is absent. BIA’s live directory still points to this notice. Supports a dated list comparison, not a finding that any particular petition was denied. Supporting status check outside the substantive count.

proposedParagraphs.title: Reading present community voices
proposedParagraphs.text: The contemporary Adai Caddo Indian Nation presents itself through family relationships, cultural teaching and connections with the Robeline area. Its history page combines its own voice with older published accounts. Read it as community public history, while checking particular colonial dates, linguistic classifications and land claims against the underlying records.

proposedParagraphs.title: Institutions and responsibilities
proposedParagraphs.text: The bylaws effective March 2, 2024 name the corporation Caddo Adais Indians, Inc., with Adai Caddo Indian Nation among its public names. They distribute responsibilities among six council offices, prescribed elections and appointed officers. A Council of Elders advises on social and cultural activities, youth mentoring and elders’ needs. These published rules reveal how the contemporary organization assigns work and preserves records; they should not be treated as an unchanged model of historical Adai government.

proposedParagraphs.title: Language reconstruction as current work
proposedParagraphs.text: The organization describes rebuilding Adaizan teaching materials from the limited surviving documentation, comparing John Sibley’s spellings and deriving a writing system. Its programs page reports translations and instructional videos, with a dictionary and children’s book still underway. This is an account of contemporary reconstruction and teaching ambitions. It supplies neither a current speaker census nor independent agreement on the historical language’s classification.

proposedParagraphs.title: Teaching and practical community services
proposedParagraphs.text: The programs page describes member-led history and culture seminars at quarterly council meetings, along with field trips. It also describes a volunteer emergency-management program offering supplies, training and communications resources to members and neighbors. These are the organization’s descriptions of its activities and capacity; they do not by themselves measure participation, educational outcomes or emergency readiness.

proposedParagraphs.title: Learning through public history visits
proposedParagraphs.text: A March 31, 2026 report describes a weeklong trip through public historical and cultural institutions in the Natchitoches region. Organizer Robert Brevelle framed the visits around education and relationships with ancestors and land, while historian Dee Niette Thompson thanked participating institutions. This dated report makes the field-trip program more concrete. Its historical and genealogical assertions still need their own evidence.

proposedParagraphs.title: Kinship, mobility and church life
proposedParagraphs.text: An undated briefing prepared by historian Michael Lawson with Rufus Davis and anthropologist Maria Wade describes relatives living away who return for family occasions. Its later pages connect Depression-era and wartime work migration with continuing visits, church and homecoming. The community’s current history page also gives Catholic faith a prominent place. Together these sources offer attributed accounts of connection across distance, rather than proof that every family shares one religious experience or an identical migration history.

proposedParagraphs.title: Acknowledgment in a participant’s words
proposedParagraphs.text: In a May 2025 Native America Calling interview, council member Robert Brevelle connected federal acknowledgment with elder health care, young people’s education and cultural preservation. He also described the cost and specialized work involved in pursuing acknowledgment. The tribal-posted transcript preserves these priorities in an identified participant’s voice. His hopes and account of the process should be distinguished from an agency ruling, current petition status or grants actually awarded.

optionalSupportingParagraphs.title: Keeping state and federal listings distinct
optionalSupportingParagraphs.text: On October 20, 2026, Louisiana’s official directory listed Adai Caddo Indians of Louisiana among the state-recognized tribes. The BIA notice published January 30, 2026 lists Caddo Nation of Oklahoma and contains no Adai entry; the BIA’s live directory still links that notice. These are distinct political names and recognition records, rather than interchangeable labels.

optionalSupportingParagraphs.title: Public interpretation and a public facility
optionalSupportingParagraphs.text: The organization’s explanation of its seal, attributed to Paige Holsapple and Robert Brevelle, links particular motifs with its historical memory and faith. It is the community’s interpretation of this seal, rather than a universal code for Caddo designs. A separate short page describes its cultural center near Robeline as a museum and meeting facility; that public institution should be distinguished from a historical territorial boundary.

geographicFindings.name: Adai Caddo Indian Nation Cultural Center
geographicFindings.featureType: Public cultural center and meeting facility
geographicFindings.precision: Published public street address only; not geocoded
geographicFindings.qualification: State directory prints LA-486 instead of community LA-485. Preserve this discrepancy before later geocoding. No ancestral boundary, private site or cemetery coordinates inferred.

countRecommendation.note: Replace the existing About directory with the substantive History page and enrich the existing Programs source. Those two are replacements/enrichment, not two wholly new count increments. Count article/PDF mirror and radio episode/transcript as one work each. Do not add supporting listings merely to reach a quota.

researchGaps: Independent language scholarship must evaluate the historical Adai classification; the community program page’s Caddoan certainty is not consensus evidence.
No current federal acknowledgment petition disposition, denial or complete documentary petition was verified here. The official current-linked list supports dated absence only.
The Newberry briefing’s grant and cession dates disagree internally; land-title chronology needs the actual instruments and specialist work.
Earlier and current membership figures use different dates and potentially different definitions; no demographic trend is inferred.
Public cultural-center road number conflicts with the state contact listing. Coordinates and any wider homeland mapping remain unverified.
No survey of all households’ faith, language use or teaching outcomes was located. Named public representatives’ accounts are not generalized to everyone.
integrationNotes: Historical Adai people and language, the mission/presidio called Los Adaes, the contemporary Adai Caddo organization and Caddo Nation of Oklahoma require separate descriptions.
All six substantive works are cited in proposedParagraphs. Supporting sources are only cited in the separate optionalSupportingParagraphs.
No publication date is assigned to an undated webpage or the Newberry briefing from copyright, upload date or PDF metadata.
No private mound, burial, archaeological-site coordinates, member contact information, ceremony instructions or local cache files should be exposed on the Site.
No people were contacted; no main Site/data files were modified.
